775448,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.1.5.1.1,1926-03-18,,,,stagedirection,,,,Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee tomorrow to consider the following proposed resolution:-

Resolved, That it is expedient to introduce a measure to approve of the agreement dated the sixth day of July, 1925, between the government of the Dominion of Canada and the governments of certain of His Majesty's colonies in the West Indies, which agreement is termed ""Canada-British West Indies-Bermuda-British Guiana-British Honduras Trade Agreement, 1925,"" and to provide:-

column2: That after the said agreement is brought into force, and so long as it remains in force, goods mentioned in the said agreement, the produce or manufacture of any of the colonies parties to the said agreement, which are conveyed without transshipment, except transshipment at a port of any of the said colonies, by ship direct into a sea or river port of Canada, shall be admitted to Canada at the rates of duties provided in the said agreement.

That the tariff concessions covered by the said agreement to he extended to goods the produce or manufacture of any of the said colonies shall be so extended with respect to any one or more of the said colonies which may have ratified the said agreement on and after a day to be fixed by proclamation of the Governor in Council, which proclamation shall be published in the Canada Gazette.
That subject to the provisions of the Customs Tariff, 1907, the Governor in Council may, by order in council, extend the said advantages to goods the produce or manufacture of any British country.

That the operation of all laws inconsistent with the giving to the provisions of the said agreement and of any act that may be founded on this resolution their full effect shall from time to time be suspended to the extent of such inconsistencies.

That subject to the ratification of the said agreement by the various colonies which are parties thereto, and to the fulfilment of their undertaking to make the contributions on their behalf as specified therein, the Governor in Council be empowered to make such arrangements as may be necessary to carry out the provisions of the said agreement relating to the establishment of steamship services between Canada and the colonies concerned, and any expenses incurred in carrying out the said agreement shall be defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for that purpose.

775452,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.1.7.1.1,1926-03-18,,,,stagedirection,,,,Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (for the Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization) moved that the House go into committee to-morrow to consider the following proposed resolution:-
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to authorize advances to settlers on crown lands, and to provide:-

column2: That for purposes connected with settlement, the minister may make loans to settlers on the basis of improvement of land and farm buildings erected-
to a settler who is a Canadian citizen as that term is defined in the Immigration Act, an amount not exceeding $1,000, (b) to a settler other than a Canadian citizen an amount not exceeding $500.
That settlement loans under the proposed legislation shall not exceed the sum of $5,000,000 in any fiscal year, and shall be paid out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund.

That Settlement Loan committees may .be established anywhere in Canada to report upon and recommend to the minister the suitability of a settler, and of any parcel of crown land, and to advise the minister as to the amount of loan to be made and how it should be expended, and such committee shall consist of not less than two nor more than three, persons in the employ of the Dominion government or of any provincial government, such persons to be nominated by the minister, one of whom shall be the Dominion lands agent or the provincial crown lands agent, as the case may be, for the district in which the settler is located, and no salary or remuneration additional to that which he otherwise receives shall be paid to members of such committee.

That no settlement loan shall be made unless recommended by a Settlement Loan committee, and unless approved by the minister, nor until the applicant ' has been recommended by a committee as a suitable settler and the land as suitable for settlement for agricultural purposes, and all settlement loans shall be expended under the direction of the minister.

That no settlement loan shall be made upon the security of improvements upon any provincial crown land, unless the province by appropriate legislation, has provided that the improvements upon the security of which any such loan is made shall be subject to a first charge for the amount of such loan with interest, and that no patent shall be issued for the said land until such loan with interest is repaid in full.

That the payment of principal shall be made in annual instalments extending over a period of not more than ten years from the date the settlement loan is made, the first payment to become due and payable two years from the date of the settlement loan, provided that the settler may at any time repay the whole of the settlement loan with interest to date of payment, and all loans shall bear interest at the rate of five per cent per annum, payable on the respective dates upon which instalments of principal fall due.

That when a settlement loan has been made upon the security of improvements upon Dominion crown lands, the patent shall not issue until the loan and all interest charges thereon have been paid in full. [DOT]
That if a provincial government, not having suit-ble crown lands available, acquires by purchase suitable

column1: lands for settlement under the provisions of this legislation, the minister may pay to a provincial government a sum not exceeding one-half of the interest on the purchase price of such lands, reckoned at five per centum per annum, for a period not exceeding two years from the date of settlement.

column2: That the Governor in Council may, on the recommendation of the minister, make regulations to carry out these provisions, and the minister shall make an annual report to parliament of all operations under the proposed legislation.

775460,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.1.9.1.1,1926-03-18,,,,stagedirection,,,,"Hon. J. H. KING (Kootenay, Acting Minister of Labour) moved that the House go into committee to-morrow to consider the following .proposed resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting Old Age Pensions, and to provide,-

column2: That the Governor in Council may make an agreement with the Lieutenant-Governor in Council of any province for the payment to such province quarterly of an amount equal to one-half of the net sum paid out during the preceding quarter by such province for pensions pursuant to a provincial statute authorizing and providing for the payment of such pensions to the persons and under the conditions hereinafter specified and regulations made under the proposed legislation.

That every agreement so made shall continue in force so long as the provincial statute remains in operation or until after the expiration of ten years from the date upon which notice of an intention to determine the agreement is given by the Governor Genleral to the Lieutenant-Governor of the province with w*hich the same was made.

That before any agreement so made comes into operation, the Governor in Council shall approve the scheme for the administration of pensions proposed to be adopted by the province, and no change in such scheme shall be made by the province without the consent of th6 Governor in Council.

That all sums payable to any province in pursuance of any such agreement shall be payable from time to time on the certificate of the Treasury Board out of any moneys belonging to the consolidated revenue fund of Canada not otherwise appropriated, and the Governor in Council may bor-

column1: row from time to time such sums as may be required for the purpose of making such payments.

column2: That provision shall be made for the payment of a pension to every person who, at the date of the proposed commencement of the pension:-
is a British subject, or, being a widow, was such before her marriage;
has attained the age of seventy years;
has resided in Canada for the twenty years immediately preceding the date aforesaid;
has resided in the province in which the application for pension is made for the five years immediately preceding the said date;
is not an Indian as defined by the Indian Act;
has not made any voluntary assignment or transfer of property for the purpose of qualifying for a pension.
That the receipt of a pension shall not by itself constitute a disqualification from voting at any provincial or municipal election.

That the maximum pension payable shall be two hundred and forty dollars yearly, which shall be subject to reduction by the amount of the income of the pensioner in excess of one hundred and twenty-five dollars a year.

That provisions be made as to the credit to the pension authority of the annual value of a pensioner's residence, and the recovery of pension payments out of deceased pensioner's estate, and for the distribution of pension burden among provinces by proportionate reimbursement or proportionate reduction where the pensioner resided in more than one province or transfers his permanent residence to another province, and for ceasing payments where he transfers his residence to some place out of Canada, and the revival of his rights upon again becoming a resident of Canada^
That no pension shall be subject to alienation or transfer by the pensioner, or to seizure in satisfaction of any claim against him.

That on or before the thirtieth day of April in each year, the Minister of Finance shall make a full report to parliament of the operation of the agreements made pursuant to the proposed act, and of the moneys of Canada paid to /the provinces under each of the several agreements entered into pursuant thereto.

That the Governor in Council shall have power from time to time, on the recommendation of the Minister of Labour, and with the approval of the Treasury Board, to make regulations, not inconsistent with the provisions of the proposed act, with regard to the pensions herein provided for, and such regulations shall be published in the Canada Gazette, and be laid before parliament.

I understand that Australian and New Zealand butter is being sold in Canada in such a way that the consumer thinks he is getting the Canadian made product. 775481,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.2.2,1926-03-18,ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916,ca.m.1883,Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):,,PRIVILEGE-MR. WOODSWORTH,,,I rise to a question of privilege.

My attention has been called to misleading reports of an incident that occurred on the night the House adjourned. The story was first published, I believe, by the Toronto Mail and Empire, and has since been added to and embellished by other papers. A typical account is given by the Daily Intelligencer of Belleville of March 6, where I note under the motto ""Let there be harmony in things essential-liberty in things not essential- charity in all,"" there is an editorial dealing with ""Ottawa's unholy trio."" Attention is called to-

The most remarkable and illuminating spectacle of 'three anti-British members of the Commons, Messrs. Woodsworth and Heaps of Winnipeg, and Bourassa of Montreal, remaining sullenly seated while the national anthem was sung in the House.
Later on the article goes on to say:
It was South Hastings' member who started the loyal anthem and prayer for His Majesty as the House was recessing. W. Ernest Tummon, M.P., as all
Canada knows by this time, is a singer
As the critical moment approached-
I do not know what critical moment is referred to.
-some one said: "" Come on, Ernie (they call him that) start 'The King'

He did. It was a notable event. Many said they never remembered the national anthem being sung in the House before. Everyone at once got to his feet, even the galleries joining, in this tribute of respect to His Majesty, except the unholy trio.

Hon. members will recall that in connection with the divisions, there was considerable confusion, various groups singing rival songs such as ""Alouette"", ""There's a long, long trail awinding"" and so on. Not being a singer, I did not participate in this, but I was in conversation with my neighbour the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). I remember that I became conscious that the tune was ""God Save the King"" but I paid no attention. Por me it was part of the
exuberant but rather undignified performance.

I think I was not far wrong as I have since been informed that after ""God Save the King"" was sung a group of members on this side of the House started ""O Canada"", during the singing of vfhich many members on the other side left the chamber. Personally I attach no significance to this. There was general confusion; the House was dispersing.
I may say however that the report was quite inaccurate for my colleague from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) was standing while the national anthem was being sung.

,Labour,,James Shaver Woodsworth,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916&Language=E&Section=ALL
775482,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.2.3,1926-03-18,intervention,,,,PRIVILEGE-MR. WOODSWORTH,,,He was not.

Supply-Customs

investigator. It will be seen that the facts as submitted by the hon. member are absolutely correct, with the exception that the four cars in question were headed from Canada to the United States, instead of from the United States to Canada. That is not an excuse, and I am not urging it as such. There should be an export entry for any goods exported from the United States; those cars should have reported at the customs, and there was only one man in charge at, the time. I am glad to say that the deputy minister yesterday forwarded to the collector of customs and excise at Niagara Falls, Ontario, the following telegram.
You are instructed to assign two officers to night duty at Queenston bridge on and after tihe 18th instant.

The hon. member for East Essex (Mr. Morand) made an inquiry concerning the appointment of an officer at Tilbury, Ontario, and in reply to his question I informed him that Mr. W. A. Hutton and terminated his services there on December 2, 1925 and that I was under the impression that a relieving officer was in charge of that port. Upon investigation at the department I find that Mr. M. W. Richards was appointed by the Civil Service Commission and took charge of that port on January 5, 1926. I will send over to the hon. member a copy of the advertisement for the position and a copy of all the correspondence exchanged between the Civil Service Commission and the department in connection with the appointment.

The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) asked to be supplied with a list showing the retirements under the Civil Service Superannuation Act of 1924, in the Department of Customs and Excise. I have had the list prepared, and am handing it to my hon. friend. It includes both the inside and the outside service.

775525,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.6.8,1926-03-18,493aa226-db5b-4eff-854d-21fbed53bcca,ca.m.3576,Mr. McGEBBON:,,LIST OF OFFICES AND SUB-OFFICES IN ONTARIO FROM WHICH VESSELS ARRIVE AND DEPART,,,Before the minister

leaves that subject, I should like to bring to his attention the inconvenience that Canadian citizens often have to suffer when returning from a visit to the United States. I would call his attention particularly to the action of his officials at Bridgeburg. In the last year or two I have had to 4 p.m. bring to the notice of the department a number of occasions when Canadian citizens have been detained in a

rather high-handed and ruthless manner by the officials and put to a great deal of inconvenience. Perhaps he will inform the committee what instructions his officials have in that regard?

775526,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.6.9,1926-03-18,20153f1d-4d12-4d52-b34f-744ffb0e1cd0,ca.m.7879,Mr. BOIVIN:,Minister of Customs and Excise,LIST OF OFFICES AND SUB-OFFICES IN ONTARIO FROM WHICH VESSELS ARRIVE AND DEPART,,,I can assure my hon. friend that the officers of the Department of Customs have always been instructed by the officers of the department here to treat not only home-coming Canadians but persons from all countries entering Canada with the utmost possible courtesy. It is quite possible -I am not disputing what my hon. friend says-that there has been a lack of courtesy and perhaps actual rudeness on the part of some of our officers. Two cases of that nature, and only two, have been reported to me since I took charge of the department. An investigation was made, a disciplinary warning was given to the officers concerned and the inspector communicated with the persons who had complained of discourtesy and made the required apologies. If my hon. friend can give me the name of any officer who has failed in his duty in this respect, I shall be only too glad to investigate. It is possible, however, that the blame is not entirely on the officers of my department. In one or two other cases reported, officers of the Immigration department had lacked tact and courtesy. If my hon. friend will either himself or through any of his friends give me specific cases, I promise that they shall receive prompt and thorough investigation.

Mr. MeGIBBON: Mr. Chairman, I simply bring this matter to the attention of the minister because on a number of occasions I have had to bring to the attention of the department complaints by home-coming Canadians, who, although they carried letters of identification in order to avoid that very trouble, were detained, some of them for hours, some of them for days, and treated in a rather rude manner. The minister will find those letters in the department.

Mr. BCflVIN: If their right to enter Canada was questioned in spite of the letters of identification which they carried, they were undoubtedly detained by the officers of the Department of Immigration. AVe have no control whatever over those officers, but I will bring the matter to the attention of the Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Stewart). There is no more excuse for the immigration officers than there would be for customs officers to be discourteous to home-coming Canadians.

775527,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.6.10,1926-03-18,ca28dee6-12e2-47ac-ab0a-584fb493a400,ca.m.3672,Mr. MORAND:,,LIST OF OFFICES AND SUB-OFFICES IN ONTARIO FROM WHICH VESSELS ARRIVE AND DEPART,,,Mr. Chairman, as I notice the Minister of Customs is very anxious to save money, I wonder if he has ever thought of the feasibility of combining the immigration and customs officials at the port of AVindsor? AVe have there two different sets of officers, under two different departments, doing work that could easily be done by the same men. I do not want to see these men put out of employment, but it seems to me that in course of time, instead of appointing new men under two different departments, the work could be combined and done' quite effectively by one set of men. That would also save a lot of trouble to the people passing backwards and forwards between Detroit and AVindsor, many thousands of whom are crossing every day. I was just wondering whether this had ever been thought of, because it does seem to me that is one place where something could be saved.

There is another thing that strikes me particularly with regard to that port, where we have a very large customs entry. I am told, and I believe I am credibly informed, that when an officer at that particular port requires even a whisk, it is necessary for him to send in a requisition to the department at Ottawa, and wait perhaps two or three weeks for authorization to buy a small article of that kind. I think a small amount of petty cash should be kept on hand at the local office for this purpose, .to save the time of the officers filling in requisitions for small articles of this kind.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Raymond Ducharme Morand,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ca28dee6-12e2-47ac-ab0a-584fb493a400&Language=E&Section=ALL
775528,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.6.11,1926-03-18,20153f1d-4d12-4d52-b34f-744ffb0e1cd0,ca.m.7879,Mr. BOIVIN:,Minister of Customs and Excise,LIST OF OFFICES AND SUB-OFFICES IN ONTARIO FROM WHICH VESSELS ARRIVE AND DEPART,,,Answering the last question first, I might tell my hon. friend that the custom which he complains of is one that has existed almost from time immemorial in connection with all customs ports. It has always been necessary for the officers requiring supplies to send in their requisitions to the department at Ottawa, and either have the supplies forwarded to them from Ottawa or obtain authorization to purchase. The suggestion made by my hon. friend is well worthy of consideration, and it will be considered not as regards supplies of value or importance, but for the petty articles such as whisks, hammers, brooms, and other supplies,, that may be required. I think a small cash allowance could be given to the local officers for this purpose.

We have often seriously considered the combination of the servioes of customs and-immigration but it has been found practically impossible to do this at the larger ports. The duties of the two sets of officers are entirely different. Their responsibilities are entirely different, and their training requires to>
Supply-Customs

be entirely different. It is true that the practice has been adopted and this economy effected at very small frontier ports where very few people cross the boundary, and where there is only a small quantity of goods to be examined. There are some small ports where part of the officer's salary is paid by one department and part by the other. The officer reports to both departments. It has been found impossible so far, in connection with the larger ports, to combine the officers doing the two different kinds of work in the same department.

,Liberal,,Georges Henri Boivin,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=20153f1d-4d12-4d52-b34f-744ffb0e1cd0&Language=E&Section=ALL
775529,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.6.12,1926-03-18,b9befc64-819d-4523-8a07-915e74257442,ca.m.5903,Mr. HANSON:,,LIST OF OFFICES AND SUB-OFFICES IN ONTARIO FROM WHICH VESSELS ARRIVE AND DEPART,,,I thought it was the well established view of the department that that should be done as far as possible. I remember a case in the province of New Brunswick not very long ago where an official of the Immigration department was let out on the ground that his sendees could be performed by an officer of the Customs department. I have in mind the port of McAdam, which is quite an important port of entry on the frontier between New Brunswick and Maine, where there are two sets of officers, and where I fancy the work of the immigration officers occupies only a little time morning and evening when the trains are coming across the frontier. I do not see any reason why in the course of time these two positions should not be more or less amalgamated and the same officers perform both services. The customs work at that point is no doubt more important than the work of the immigration officers, but a very considerable saving could be effected there, and I hope the minister will take that into consideration.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Richard Burpee Hanson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9befc64-819d-4523-8a07-915e74257442&Language=E&Section=ALL
775530,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.6.13,1926-03-18,20153f1d-4d12-4d52-b34f-744ffb0e1cd0,ca.m.7879,Mr. BOIVIN:,Minister of Customs and Excise,LIST OF OFFICES AND SUB-OFFICES IN ONTARIO FROM WHICH VESSELS ARRIVE AND DEPART,,,The matter will receive further consideration when the session is over; of course, it will be impossible to consider it at the present time. The information my hon. friend has just given to the House is absolutely correct. The officer in question was removed and his duties were assigned to the officer representing the Department of Customs at that port. This action confirms to a certain extent the statement I made a moment ago regarding the smaller ports where one officer was charged with doing both customs and immigration work.

,Liberal,,Georges Henri Boivin,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=20153f1d-4d12-4d52-b34f-744ffb0e1cd0&Language=E&Section=ALL
775531,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.6.14,1926-03-18,b9befc64-819d-4523-8a07-915e74257442,ca.m.5903,Mr. HANSON:,,LIST OF OFFICES AND SUB-OFFICES IN ONTARIO FROM WHICH VESSELS ARRIVE AND DEPART,,,I would like to ask a

question which perhaps does not come under this particular item; but I am sorry I was not here when the estimates were before the House a day or so ago, with reference to the preventive service in the bay of Fundy. What boats are employed there, how large are they, and is it the intention of the government to augment this service. The reason I ask is that one day in 14011-106i

the month of October last I had the duty to perform of going to the island of Grand Manan to assist in the happy return of my hon. friend the member for Charlotte (Mr. Grimmer), and on our way out, I was in the pilot house of the steamboat, and the captain pointed out to me three boats in the distance which he said, and I have no doubt he was correct, were rum runners which had been located there for several weeks, plying their illicit traffic with the people on shore without let or hindrance by any officer of this government.' I had it in mind at the time to communicate with the department, but under the stress of the election I did not do so. I would point out to the minister that practically during the whole of the summer and autumn season of 1925 bootleggers were in the bay of Fundy plying their illicit traffic, delivering their goods, taking the money of the people, and so far as those from whom I inquired knew, there had not been a single vessel or boat of the customs preventive service in the bay of Fundy waters during that whole period. These people were not in any way interferred with, and they were in those waters till the autumn gales came on. Now that is something that should not continue. Possibly this statement of facts, or what have been detailed to me as facts, will enable the department to give some consideration and attention to that sheet of water next year, for certainly something ought to be done there. I happen to know, not from personal knowledge, but from information that has reached me, that there is a considerable volume of illicit liquor smuggling on the bay of Fundy coast, and no doubt the revenues of this country have in that way been deprived of very large sums of money. Some of this liquor is destined for conveyance to the neighbouring state of Maine, some of it is for local consumption, but I imagine that the most of it is for export, because we are rather a sober people down in that part of the country. I hope the minister will give this matter his attention, and that in the spring season now opening this situation will be looked into and this evil remedied.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Richard Burpee Hanson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9befc64-819d-4523-8a07-915e74257442&Language=E&Section=ALL
775532,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.6.15,1926-03-18,20153f1d-4d12-4d52-b34f-744ffb0e1cd0,ca.m.7879,Mr. BOIVIN:,Minister of Customs and Excise,LIST OF OFFICES AND SUB-OFFICES IN ONTARIO FROM WHICH VESSELS ARRIVE AND DEPART,,,When these estimates were

last 'before the committee, I myself stated that we were not satisfied with the preventive service that we now have on the coasts of the three Maritime provinces. The nearest boat we have to the bay of Fundy is one mentioned in the list which I gave to the hon. member for West York on page 1634 of Hansard. Patrol Boat G, with headquarters at Yarmouth, Nova Scotia. It is impossible for that boat to carry on a patrol service in the bay df Fundy as it should be carried on but I promise the hon. gentleman that the
Supply-Customs

service will be improved' during the present season. I would go further and tell him that if he has any information which might lead to the conviction of the men involved, in addition to the information he has just given to the House, I should; be glad' to receive it confidentially. If that information can bring about a prosecution it is not yet too late to institute proceedings.

775533,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.6.16,1926-03-18,2cf93f16-ac02-4963-ae74-f74b1cb23251,ca.m.6710,Mr. FOSTER:,,LIST OF OFFICES AND SUB-OFFICES IN ONTARIO FROM WHICH VESSELS ARRIVE AND DEPART,,,SWbat special instructions

are given to the customs officers at the various ports. on the Atlantic coast of the Maritimes in regard to smuggling operations? Are there any Special instructions beyond those contained in the general clauses of the Customs Act?

,Conservative (1867-1942),,George Eulas Foster,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=2cf93f16-ac02-4963-ae74-f74b1cb23251&Language=E&Section=ALL
775534,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.6.17,1926-03-18,20153f1d-4d12-4d52-b34f-744ffb0e1cd0,ca.m.7879,Mr. BOIVIN:,Minister of Customs and Excise,LIST OF OFFICES AND SUB-OFFICES IN ONTARIO FROM WHICH VESSELS ARRIVE AND DEPART,,,The preventive officersin fact all the officers of the department having power to make seizures-are given instructions in advance to Seize and detain goods they may catch persons in the act of smuggling, goods which may have been smuggled into Canada. In addition to the generail instructions concerning the seizure of goods which must be reported to Ottawa, special instructions were issued by the department on July 3, 1625, after the Customs Act was amended last session. The memorandum reads as follows:

There is printed herewith copy of an act to amend the Customs Act assented to by iparilitament on the 2?th of June, 1925. This act provides for the repeal of sections 206 and 219 of the Customs Act, and the substitution 'therefor of new sections bearing the same numbers wherein provision is made for 'imposing heavier fines and imprisonment (for the offences of smuggling and of keeping or selling goods unlawfully imported, wiith further provision making it an indictable offence to smuggle goods or keep or sell unlawfully imported goods of the value of $200 or over. In respect of the latter offences you are instructed that in all cases where you are satisfied the goods were smuggled for personal use and not ifor business use and it is a first offence, not to commence any proceedings Iby way o<f indictment without first communicating the fact ""to the department and awaiting instructions. 'In all other cases proceedings are to be taken forthwith.

That means that the deputy minister with the authorization of the then acting minister, sent instructions to all collectors in the country that whenever smuggling, or keeping smuggled goods of a value of more than $200 for commercial purposes came to their attention they were to prosecute before the courts at onoe without communicating with headquarters at Ottawa.

,Liberal,,Georges Henri Boivin,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=20153f1d-4d12-4d52-b34f-744ffb0e1cd0&Language=E&Section=ALL
775535,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.6.18,1926-03-18,2cf93f16-ac02-4963-ae74-f74b1cb23251,ca.m.6710,Mr. FOSTER:,,LIST OF OFFICES AND SUB-OFFICES IN ONTARIO FROM WHICH VESSELS ARRIVE AND DEPART,,,Let me .put this case to

the minister. Suppose a customs official is advised that a ship is in the harbour with liquor on board which is intended to be landed, and in view of that information he went elsewhere looking for liquor to be

landed at another cove some miles away where there was no liquor and none expected to be landed. It was not certain that the landing was to be made at the latter spot; on the contrary the officer knew it was not expected there. If such facts as these were 'brought to the attention of the1, minister would he consider the advisability of dismissing the officer for acting in such a manner?

,Conservative (1867-1942),,George Eulas Foster,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=2cf93f16-ac02-4963-ae74-f74b1cb23251&Language=E&Section=ALL
775536,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.6.19,1926-03-18,20153f1d-4d12-4d52-b34f-744ffb0e1cd0,ca.m.7879,Mr. BOIVIN:,Minister of Customs and Excise,LIST OF OFFICES AND SUB-OFFICES IN ONTARIO FROM WHICH VESSELS ARRIVE AND DEPART,,,If the name of the officer

special staff. I desire to make myself clear. The men authorized by the $350,000 vote of last year were roughly estimated at 200. Only 67 were appointed. Those who will be retained out of the 67 so appointed will be included in this number of approximately 260. These of course are just approximate numbers. The idea would be to group the men by twos and threes at junction points where [DOT]several routes coming in from the United States converge to go into one large city; for instance at the Victoria bridge at Montreal, or at the Longueuil ferry. We would thus have a double check on all the incoming cars at these particular strategic points. In addition to that,
Supply-Customs

I think that a certain number of officers should be equipped with motor cycfles or high powered ears for the purpose of patrolling, [DOT] what I might almost call, the lonely country roads, the unimproved dirt, roads that cross the boundary 'between the United States and Canada. They are or can be used by smugglers during the dry season of the year, but there is so little traffic that it would never pay to appoint permanent officers to guard them. In that way, we can pretty well protect the boundary. Hon. gentlemen will notice there is a less number of men mentioned in my estimate for the province oif Ontario than for the province of Quebec. There is an extensive land boundary between the United States and the Province of Quebec, whereas the boundary line between Ontario and the United States is formed almost entirely by water. The points at which people can cross and come into Ontario are not so numerous as they are in Quebec. I would adopt the same methods along the boundary of the province of Manitoba at and near Emerson, and upon all the different roads leading up from the United States to the city of Winnipeg. The same thing applies also at points south of Vancouver, between Washington and BritiSh Columbia. I do not think this will be necessary between the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan and the United States, because there is very little smuggling done there. I am told that the distance between the large American cities on the south and the large Canadian cities on the north of the boundary line, is so great that it is not advantageous for smugglers to try 'to operate in that territory. The service will also have to be increased on 'the Pacific and- Atlantic coasts. We had fourteen boats on the Atlantic coast. That number is not sufficient. The only way to effectively interfere' with smuggling on the coast is by the use of patrol boats. A great number of boats have been offered to us for rental, but I have not rented more than one or two so far. A great many of the boats offered to us for rental are boats having a speed of about eight or nine knots per hour, and naturally they would be of little use in preventing smuggling.

The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, mentioned the fact that we had only made forty seizures during the past year. It is not the duty of patrol boats to make seizures and we cannot expect that service from them. The patrol boat is operating to scare the smugglers away, to prevent any communication between the coast and the liquor-laden schooner outside of the three-mile limit. When
fMr. Boivin.]

patrol boats are operating very few attempts are made to unload cargoes, and when vessels are obliged to remain too long on the open sea with their cargoes, they naturally move on and endeavour to send it into the United States or sometimes deliver it at Newfoundland 'points. The efficiency of the patrol service should never be measured by the number of seizures, but a certain number of boats should be added to the service. In British Columbia certain boats should also be used. The coast of Vancouver island should be protected although there is not much smuggling into Vancouver island, the largest amount of smuggling being into the bays and inlets on the coast of continental British Columbia. We have only one cruiser there; we should have others and I hope as soon as possible three or four other boats may be placed in operation. I hope I can lease boats to prove that this is a means of prevention. Later on if the experiment is successful I intend to ask parliament to vote a sufficient sum of money to build a certain number of fast patrol boats. They need not be very large, but they must be fast, because a patrol boat, if it is to be of any use, must be fast.

The reason why we have not made provision fot patrolling the Great Lakes is that we consider that most of the ports at which boats of any size or importance land are already protected by preventive officers. The great trouble on the Great Lakes is not so much the smuggling in as the smuggling out. A great deal of liquor, as we all know, is shipped from lake ports to the United States of America, but we are particular about the export entry, about the necessity of giving the name of the boat and a description of the cargo in each instance, so that we may have some control of the boats when they come back and make sure that they do not return laden with United States merchandise. The boats report back empty to customs officers along the coast, and there must therefore be very little incentive for any one who is not exporting from Canada to the United States to use small boats for the purpose of smuggling goods into this country. The coast line of the Great Lakes is fairly well protected now by preventive officers, by sub-ports

and ports and we do not consider it necessary at the present time to put patrol boats on the Great Lakes. I thank the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) for bringing the matter before the committee.

An idea which has been submitted to me by one of the officials of my department is that of erecting steel gates on roads crossing the boundary, gates which might be locked at sunset and opened at sunrise, and watched over perhaps by one preventive officer. 775558,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.6.41,1926-03-18,20153f1d-4d12-4d52-b34f-744ffb0e1cd0,ca.m.7879,Mr. BOIVIN:,Minister of Customs and Excise,LIST OF OFFICES AND SUB-OFFICES IN ONTARIO FROM WHICH VESSELS ARRIVE AND DEPART,,,True; that is exactly what I have said. For a great many positions you cannot get a better appointing authority than the Civil Service Commission. But I say there are some positions of a peculiar nature requiring certain qualifications which cannot be established by a man's .examination paper, that cannot even be manifested by his appearance, yet these positions the Civil Service Commission are called upon to fill. Let me give an example. There is no man in this country prouder of a certain branch of the government service than the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), sitting beside me. I think every member, be he Conservative, Liberal, Progressive, Labour or Independent, shares his pride in the achievements and reputation of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. In .the customs 5 p.m. inquiry and elsewhere it has been said, ""Oh, why don't you assign this work to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police?"" And in every case where that branch has been placed in charge of any particular

work which came within their jurisdiction it has been done excellently. Now, I ask hon. members on the other side this question-and excuse me, Mr. Chairman, if I put it direct- Will any one rise in his place and say that appointments to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police should be made by the Civil Service Commission?

It is so in the Old Country in connection with the police, or with any similar semi-military body. Therefore that illustration does not at all come fairly within the purview of the minister's answer.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Ambrose Upton Gledstanes Bury,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=29f4a12d-1127-490f-9ae1-2d9ac93671eb&Language=E&Section=ALL
775562,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.6.45,1926-03-18,20153f1d-4d12-4d52-b34f-744ffb0e1cd0,ca.m.7879,Mr. BOIVIN:,Minister of Customs and Excise,LIST OF OFFICES AND SUB-OFFICES IN ONTARIO FROM WHICH VESSELS ARRIVE AND DEPART,,,Perhaps my hon. friend did not hear the preliminary part of my remarks.
I
column2: did not say to the Civil Service Commission, ""Hands off the Customs department."" I agree that the commission should continue to make a large number of the appointments- appointments of customs collectors, appointments of customs officers here at Ottawa, appointments of appraisers, and so on. I am now referring to the new preventive service, and I think it should be a semi-military or semi-police service. I say that that service cannot be satisfactorily appointed by the Civil Service Commission. I hope the committee and the House will not decide otherwise. I will not however determine any definite plan of action until I have received the report of the committee. It will render effective service to the country if it only determines where some of the smuggling takes place at the present time and reports to the House ways and means of organizing an efficient preventive service to stop that smuggling. If it can do this it will do better than any special committee that has been appointed by this parliament for many years.

They did not cariy in connection with the Kingsville appointment. Is the minister aware that all papers and information submitted to him by the department in connection with the dismissal of Mr. C.
column2: R. McCallum and the appointment of A.

column1: D.
column2: Pearsall, were issued even before Mr. Mc-Callum's appointment was made? I am impressed by the minister's desire to be fair. He said in the House some time ago that when charges were instituted against any civil servant, the procedure followed was first to suspend the man charged, and then to investigate the charges; if found guilty he would be dismissed, and if found innocent he would be reinstated. Now, I ask the minister, although this appointment did not occur during his term of office, to go back and correct mistakes where it is possible to correct them. As I have said, none of the information I requested yesterday has been supplied. The examination took place on May 29, and Mr. McCallum passed with a high percentage of marks. He had a fine reputation locally, where he was well known, and an equally fine record while on overseas service. Yet under date of June 10, 1925, I find a letter addressed to G. Graham, Esq., Assistant Inspector of Customs and Excise, Ottawa. I may use this correspondence?

I have the honour to state that the department has deemed it advisable to review the recent examination of applicants for the position of sub-collector at the outport of Kingsville.
Very remarkable that on June 10 the department should deem it necessary to review an examination that took place on May 29!
I ask the minister what happened in the meantime that the department considered it necessary that this examination should be reviewed. I might state that the person by

whom it was reviewed was a very outstanding Liberal, and the only thing in connection with the appointment that had not the appearance of political control was the examination and the marks obtained thereon. The next communication is from Mr. Graham, assistant inspector of customs and excise, under date of June 15, 1925:
In this connection I conferred with Mr. A. W. Massey, Ithe .principal of the high school at Kingsville. Ontario-
Mr. Massey, I might say, is an outstanding Liberal:

-and in the case of Mr. C. It. McCallum, I am obliged to state that this party, while of good ability, has been guilty in time past of a rather serious offence. It appears that while employed by (the Canadian Pacific Telegraph Company at Kingsville, Ontario, this party divulged certain confidential information entrusted to him, with the result that he was discharged by the telegraph company.
Mr. -Massey declined to make any change in the ratings already submitted by himself and Mr. McGuire at the previous examination.
Next I submit a letter to Mr. L. J. Lafferty, Windsor, from G. R. Kerby, chief inspector of the Canadian Pacific Railway, under date of August 15, 1925:
Dear Sir,-Further to my letter of recent date in connection with former agent C. R. McCallum.
Kindly be advised that Mr. McCallum was not discharged from the service but resigned on his own free will, not wishing to assume further responsibility as he was not acquainted with the wire work.
Under the circumstances consider he acted very wisely as our system is quite complicated which made him dependent for information from his operator.
Yours truly,
G. R. Kerby,
Inspector.
As Mr. Graham, the assistant inspector of customs and excise, points out in his letter of June 15, 1925:
Mr. Massey declined to make any change in the ratings already submitted by himself and Mr. McGuire at the previous examination.

I have the honour to state that I am this date in receipt of a report from Mr. G. Graham, Assistant Inspector of Customs and Excise, relative to the rating of the candidates who recently made application for the position of collector of customs and excise at the outport of Kingsville, Ontario.

The next is a letter to the secretary of the Civil Service Commission from Mr. R. R. Farrow, Deputy Minister, Department of Customs:

I have the honour to enclose oral examination ratings by Mr. G. C. McGuire, Inspector of Customs and Excise, and Mr. A. W. Massey, on the candidates for appointment to the .position of sub-collector of customs and excise at Kingsville, Ontario.
. The department recommends the appointment of Mr. A. D. Pearsall and copy of letter from Mr. G. Graham, Assistant Inspector of Customs and Excise-
If his position had not been stated, I would have been inclined to believe it was the Right Hon. George P. Graham, my worthy opponent in the last election. It goes on:
-is enclosed respecting the candidates, and your attention is directed to his remarks concerning Mr. McCollum , whose assignment would not be acceptable to the department.

That letter is under date of June 19. 1925, and that is the last letter which the Minister of Customs has supplied to me-one under date of June 19, 1925. Now Mr. McCallum received his official appointment under date of June 25, 1925. Here is his notification from the Civil Service Commission to report for duty. It is under date of June 25, and was received by Mr. McCallum in Kingsville on June 26:
Civil Service Commission of Canada Notification of Report for Duty Name-Charles 'R. McCallum.
Address-Kingsville, Ontario.
Department-Customs and Excise.
Branch-Kingsville, Ontario.
Title of position-Sub -collector of Customs and Excise, outport, Kingsville, Ontario.
Duties-As specified in the official definition, and such other related work as may be required.

As I said, the last letter that has been supplied to me by the minister is under date of June 19, 1925; Mr. McCallum was appointed on the 25th day of June, 192o, so it is obvious that the minister has failed in every respect to give me any papers in connection with his dismissal, and that is what I asked for yesterday.

Commission is concerned a great change has come over the minds of hon. gentlemen on both sides of this House since that body was appointed. I very distinctly remember that when the matter came up in the House- and it gives me considerable satisfaction now, although I was in a very hopeless minority at the time-I opposed the transfer of political patronage to the Civil Service Commission. I take the stand now that I took some years ago when this matter came up, that not the defeated candidate of the party in power, but the member elected, no matter to what political party he belongs, is the man who should assume full responsibility for such appointments and the advice given to the government with respect to them, and that he should stand or fall by his action. 775598,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.6.81,1926-03-18,a8b2b613-dd5c-4a22-8f22-c0e4f180c7b6,ca.m.4552,Mr. GUTHRIE:,,LIST OF OFFICES AND SUB-OFFICES IN ONTARIO FROM WHICH VESSELS ARRIVE AND DEPART,,,When this item was

under discussion on Tuesday last, the minister stated that there had been an increase in the staff of officials at Bridgeburg of some seven or eight who had been put on as car sealers at that rather important point. My object in asking a question on that occasion was to ascertain just what the facts were at Bridgeburg and also at Windsor in respect to the sealing of cars, because rumour had it that the system which had been employed at those points for some time past had been very loose and insufficient. The minister has kindly brought to the attention of the House to-day two reports made by Chief Inspector Busby of the Department of Customs and Excise, and these reports go exhaustively into the question of oar sealers at those important points, and confirm an impression which existed that little or no inspection of sealing and probqbly little or no sealing took place of cars moving on the railroads at those points between Canada and the United States.

The inspector is to be congratulated upon taking action in this matter. I see that he has recommended some seven additional car sealing inspectors at Bridgeburg, and also some six or seven at Windsor, to do work which I do not think could have been done before in. any satisfactory manner. The inspector in his report dated Bridgeburg, April 20, 1926, states-and I will not read all the report:

Accompanied by Inspector A. M. Kennedy and Supervising Officer G. A. Clark, I visited this date the Canadian National Railway freight yards at the port of Bridgeburg and ascertained that at this point during the fiscal year 1924-25 there were 209,672 cars entered Oanada and 191,132 cars were reported outward from Canada.
This is the paragraph:

The cars entering Canada at this point arrived from the Canadian National and Wabash yards at Black Rook, N.Y. Tyden. seals on such cars are stamped *with, the crown and port number by an officer at the port of Bridgeburg, and sent over to Black Rock in bundles of 1,000 to 2,000 seals to the agent o.f the railway there, where they are placed on the cars by employees of the railway company without the supervision of customs-excise officers.

That, evidently, was the system employed-sending the seals in bundles of 1,000 to 2,000 from Bridgeburg to Black Rock, where the railway employees placed them on the cars without any customs or excise inspection at all. The report continues:

These car seals are not examined by customs-excise officers 'when reported inwards at Bridgeburg, although occasionally some of such cars are examined and checked by the officer checking less than carload shipments when not engaged in checking goods out of cars which is very rarely.
The inspector very wisely recommends a change. He says:

To supervise the placing of seals on .the cars and the checking of same against inwards report, A-l, would require the services of four additional officers, two for day duty and two for night duty, to be placed in the yards of the Canadian National and Wabash railways at Black Rock, N.Y., under the supervision of Mr. Supervising Officer, G. A. Clark, at the expense of the Canadian National Railways, who would benefit thereby.

That recommendation I entirely approve. But the other branch of the report which deals with the Michigan Central railway contains no recommendation, so far as I can see. that the additional men placed in their yards shall be paid for by anyone but the government of Canada. The Canadian National for their convenience must pay for these men, but not so, if I understand the report aright, in the case of the Michigan Central. The report continues:-

We then visited the office of the Michigan Central railroad at the end of the international bridge, and examined into the manner in which train reports inwards and outwards are dealt with, and ascertained that seals have never been checked at this point, on cars entering or departing from Canada; which work is an the future to be dealt with by the four additional officers which it is proposed shall be placed at the yards of the Michigan Central railroad at Victoria.
The United States customs have officers stationed at this point-
That is, Bridgeburg.
-to examine and check seals on cars entering the United States at Black Rock, N.Y., from Bridgeburg, at the expense of the transportation companies concerned.

The United States has taken care of the situation in the interests of its government, but at the point where approximately 400,000 cars a year, 200,000 inward and 200,000 outward, cross the international bridge, no inspection in Canada of the sealing of those cars has taken place. There is an open door to smuggling. Cars unsealed entering Canada may very easily be opened in this country and goods discharged at any Canadian point, whereas these cars are supposed to be bonded going from one point in the United States through to another point, for instance Niagara Falls. The inspector is to be congratulated on having remedied that defect, which evidently was permitted to continue until some time during the last eight or ten months.
At Windsor the situation is as bad, if not worse. The inspector visited Windsor and this is what he said in his report dated April 14, 1925:
I might here state we first visited the ferry slip where the car ferries of the Wabash and Pere Marquette railways land cars for shipment to points in Canada on the Canadian Pacific Railway.

Although we waited for some time, the officer was absent from the office and could not be located, the office being open and two bunches of Tyden seals stamped with the port number were lying in the window seat of such office, where a-ny person if they so desired could take same, instead of such seals being kept under Jock and key when not being used, as they should be.

The inspector goes on to report that seven additional officers of the department are necessary to see that a proper system of sealing and inspection takes place at Windsor. In regard to the sealing of cars coming into Canada, he says he thinks this might be done as a matter of convenience at Detroit instead of on the Canadian side of the line. He continues:

This would necessitate the services of four officers for whose services the Michigan Central railroad should be required to pay. These officers to be assigned to duty in the sealing yards of the Michigan Central railroad at Detroit, two on day duty and two on night duty.
The suggestion is that the Michigan Central pay for those, as they should do, because it is for their convenience. Further on the report states:

To carry out the proper checking of seals at this point in the Michigan Central yards it will be necessary that the services of four additional officers be provided for, unless the department agrees to the placing of the four officers at Detroit (at the expense of the Michigan Central railroad) dn which event all that will be necessary will be the moving of the officers now at the electric tower to the office to be provided at the summit of the Humps, to check trains reporting inwards and outwards on forms A-l and A-5.

It will also be necessary to provide .two additional officers 'at the Wabash and Canadian 'National car ferries' slips to check seals and car numbers against reports inwards and reports outwards, which at present is not being done owing*to the insufficiency of staff to take care of this work.

I bring this to the attention of the minister because, if this system has existed until recently at important points such as Bridge-burg and Windsor, what is the situation at other international points? What is the situation at international points in Quebec and in the west? Is the loose system which obtains at Bridgeburg and Windsor also in force at the suspension bridge at Niagara Falls? Unless these cars are sealed and unless they are property inspected after being sealed, the door is thrown wide Open to all kinds of smuggling. I would strongly impress upon the minister that it be his duty or the duty of some of his officers in the near future to see that this international freight traffic is properly inspected and the cars properly sealed. If we have not enough officers now to look after the sealing, more should be appointed and their salaries paid by the railways, for whose convenience they are appointed. I personally believe that the matter
has been discussed a good deal among railway and commercial men during the past two years, and I am glad to hear that at these points there has been a remedy applied.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Hugh Guthrie,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a8b2b613-dd5c-4a22-8f22-c0e4f180c7b6&Language=E&Section=ALL

775613,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.7.1.1,1926-03-18,,,,stagedirection,,,,"Mr. G. B. NICHOLSON (East Algoma) moved the second reading of Bill No. 10, to amend The Representation Act, 1924 (Boundaries of certain constituencies).

He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill, as shown by the bill itself, is to change slightly the description of the districts of Nipissing, South Timiskaming, North Timis-kaming, East Algoma, West Algoma, and Port Arthur. The bill has been introduced because of the almost unanimous request made to the representatives of these districts by the people within the areas concerned. Without going into any considerable detail, I may say that the bill in no material way affects the population in any of the ridings concerned, and this i3 more particularly tire fact because, due to the expansion that is taking place in certain sections of northern Ontario, the population is changing so rapidly that you cannot define any particular area on a basis of population at any period and have that remain stationary for more than a few months, let alone a considerable period of years. Just let me explain how the people affected are situated in relation to the distribution of these several districts. Take first the districts of Nipissing and South Timiskaming in relation to each other. The portion of South Timiskaming, as defined in the legislation of 1924. that will be taken away

775614,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.7.1.2,1926-03-18,,,,stagedirection,,,,"and added to the district of Nipissing under this bill is a. group of townships in the northwestern corner of the district of Nipissing. In order to get in touch with their representa-ti\e in South Timiskaming the people residing in these townships must travel a distance of about 170 miles through the district of Nipissing to North Bay and then a distance of 130 to 140 miles further through the district of Nipissing on the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway to get back into that particular section in the district of South Timiskaming. They are just an isolated group of townships in one corner of the district of Timiskaming. And may I say here that I have discussed the matter with the representative of the district of Nipissing, and he agrees with me, or at least has so expressed himself, that these townships properly belong to the district of Nipissing. The only means of communication between these people and their representative now in the House and the place where they are grouped is for 200 miles across the Timagami forest reserve, or by a roundabout route of about 200 miles, all of which is through the district of Nipissing.

Let me come now to the next change that will be effected as between East Algoma and West Algoma. There is just a small group of communities with about 2,500 people in the northwestern corner of East Algoma that has been taken and put into West Algoma. Now in order for these people to get into touch with their representative who is now m the House they must travel eastward on the Canadian Pacific railway a distance of 172 miles to the town of Sudbury, and then turn westward and travel for 172 miles to Sault Ste. Marie. To put it in another way: In order for the representative of the riding to reach this particular part of his constituency he must travel through East Algoma a distance of about 340 miles. Then there is another single township where, in order for the representatives to reach that township, he must travel through East Algoma for a distance of 200 miles through a portion of the district of Nipissing, on to the district of South Timiskaming, and then for another 100 miles in East Algoma, to get to this one township.

Then in relation to the district of Port Arthur and West Algoma there is what was recognized as the southwest corner of the latter district situated about 100 miles from Sault Ste. Marie. And may I say, as most of you know, that is the centre of the district of West Algoma. In order for the representatives of these people, who now reside in Port Arthur because that place is the centre of the district of Port Arthur, to get

in touch with this particular section he must travel 280 miles eastward on the Canadian Pacific railway. Then getting into the district of West Algoma he travels about 140 miles, reaches the district of Port Arthur and then goes back again into West Algoma in order to reach this small group of communities which, as I previously stated, are 100 miles from the city of Sault Ste. Marie. I think I am well within the mark when I say that the people affected are themselves unanimous in their demand that they be replaced in the district from which, I believe, they were inadvertently removed. I think I can say that the representatives from all these districts are unanimous in their desire that the boundaries shall be restored, and that the constituencies shall bear some relation to the convenience of the people in getting in touch with their representative, and to the convenience of the representative in getting in touch with their people. I would ask, Mr. Speaker, that the bill be referred to the committee on Private Bills where the details can be fully and frankly discussed, and care taken to see that nothing of an injurious character is worked out in relation to any part of this district.",,,,

775620,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.8.2,1926-03-18,0fcd48dc-c8cd-4df7-810f-c1c29b9cb6e3,ca.m.8552,Mr. E. F. ARMSTRONG (South Timiskaming) :,,"IS, 1926 16S7",,,"Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on

this subject because it directly affects the district from which I come. Never before in the history of political divisions in the north has that district which comes near Sudbury been included in South Timiskaming. To make the situation plain to hon. members, I may say that this corner comprising about

column2: people coming within three miles of the town of Sudbury has been cut off and attached to South Timiskaming. This really means a district commencing at about Cobalt, 200 miles away. In other words this small population which, since the earliest days of settlement, has belonged to the community around the town of Sudbury, has been cut off and thrown across the forest reserve 200 miles away, and there are not fifty people between the two communities. That means that the member representing that district in Cobalt has to go 100 miles south into the Nipissing district to North Bay. Then he has to go eighty or ninety miles west to Sudbury, then take a car and go fifteen or twenty miles up through the Blizzard valley into the Capreol district. The people down there are among the finest settlers in this country. They -went in there as pioneers, they have hewn out for themselves their homes, and they very much dislike this treatment. They are associated with the conditions and problems affecting the district around Sudbury and their interests are the same. They know 14011-107i

column1: each other. They know no person in Timiskaming. They know us not at all. Our problems are not the same. We are 200 miles away and for that reason I say the present adjustment of the boundaries of that district is very unfair. On the other hand, the representative from Nipissing spoke very well along the line of representation, and I wish to say a word on that phase of the subject. Let us take the district which includes South Lorraine, Cobalt, Haileybury, New Liskeard, and that beautiful town of Engle-hart; Charlton, Gowganda, Elk Lake and Swastika, Kirkland Lake and the splendid farming community in their vicinity. Kirkland Lake alone had added a population of 4,000' or 5,000 to this district since the last redistribution. That country has picked1 up

column2: or 8,000 additional people since the last redistribution. To my mind that offsets any argument against not having sufficient population in that north district to carry the representation. I submit that the present condition is unfair to the people of both places. To run an election up there is like carrying on an election in two districts; and it is in harmony with the ideas and aspirations of the people of both the north and the south sections that they should be sent back to their old lines, the old historical community to which they belonged when they went into that country as settlers.

775621,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.8.3,1926-03-18,4d5012f1-c091-43d5-b8fc-f6f7ac8afb9c,ca.m.491,Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):,Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,IS, 1926 16S7",,,"Nobody who is unacquainted with

the geography of that particular district can discuss this matter with a large degree of intelligence, but as you know, Mr. Speaker, the matter of adjusting the boundaries of a constituency comes up after every census is taken. We have what is called the redistribution of the constituencies of Canada. It was carried through last year, indeed, in such a way as to exclude partisanship. A committee of members representing all the provinces and every party in this House sat for many weeks, or I should say many months. Sub-committees were formed. Members on both sides of the House representing every province were entrusted with the task of going over the map, of hearing representations from interested parties in the various districts, and after discussion and consideration to the fullest degree, those sub-committees agreed, and the committee itself agreed, on the redistribution that was made. A unanimous report was presented to the House, so far as I remember, and the redistribution as made was accepted unanimously by this House. Under the circumstances it is rather unusual to ask to change the boundaries of a constituency, but

am pleased to hear the minister take the very reasonable attitude he has taken in this matter. I am not affected at all and I have nothing to say against his remarks about the work of the committee last year. They had a very difficult task to perform, and I think they performed it pretty well. There was a good deal of compromising, and that is where the difficulty arose in regard to the constituencies which are now being dealt with. None of the constituencies mentioned touches my constituency, so that I am speaking not personally but simply as one from that great section of northern Ontario which requires some special consideration in a matter of this kind, consideration which the Minister of Justice has fairly agreed to give it, because the area is so immense.
If you will look at the map you will find that the area of northern Ontario, with its

column2: people or thereabouts, is a number of times greater than the area of all the rest of Ontario put together, yet there are only eight constituencies up there. I do happen to know that in the compromises which took place in the committee last year the constituency of East Algoma was changed a little, I do not mean to say unfairly, but a little unfairly to the constituency as a constituency. I am not speaking of parties. For example, without naming places, one town, the centre of East Algoma, was taken out of East Algoma and put in West Algoma and made very much more awkward to get at by virtue of that fact.

column1: As the Minister of Justice has agreed to leave this to a committee, I do not wish to take up the time of the House, but I wish to offer a suggestion. I have not discussed it with the member who proposes the bill, but I suggest that a special committee should be appointed, made up of members in proportion as to parties of course, but taking in any territory largely affected. The member for Nipissing would be one of them: it would include the other members from the district, and the committee could be balanced up with other members, if you will. I do not know whether that suggestion would be acceptable to the member who proposes the bill, but it would appear to me to be the fairest method of dealing with the matter. I have talked

the matter over with the member for East Algoma and I am convinced that his whole idea is one simply of making all of the constituencies more convenient to handle. That is something that should be taken into account where those large areas exist, because some of the constituencies up there are hundreds of miles wide and hundreds of miles long, and anything that can be done to make them a little more convenient to handle is certainly good, not only for the members who run but for the people who live in that part of the country.

MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,IS, 1926 16S7",,,"In reference to the suggestion just made by the hon. member, I think he will agree that it would be possible for hon. members specially interested to appear before the committee and make clear to its members their respective points of view. There is an objection to having a large number of special committees appointed. The House has found in the past that where there are a number of special committees, sitting frequently when the House is in session, it is a source of embarrassment, and leads to an accumulation of reports to be considered at the end of the session. We have a committee on Privileges and Elections, and its personnel is such I believe, as will commend itself to the House. There appears to be general agreement as to the propriety of referring the bill itself to a committee: I hope we may all be able to further agree to referring it to the committee on Privileges and Elections.

ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,IS, 1926 16S7",,,"There is only one precedent, so far as I can remember, and that was in 1919 when the then member for Chilliwack, Mr. Stacey, sought to have the name of his constituency changed from Chilliwack to Fraser Valley, and endeavoured to do so by way of amendment to the Representation Act. Consequently the bill is on all fours in so far as its character and status in this House are concerned. That bill was not referred to any standing or special committee; it was referred to the committee of the whole House and having passed through the committee of the whole House and third reading, it became law. There is some objection which I can understand to referring a public bill to the Private Bills committee, and if the hon. member is prepared to have the bill go to a committee at all, I do not see any objection to accepting the intimation of the leader of the House and having the bill go to the committee on Privileges and Elections.

The precedent would indicate that it should simply go through without reference to any special committee, but I take no stand on that matter. Let it go to the committee on Privileges and Elections.

775625,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.8.7,1926-03-18,255d2664-d4b3-46aa-9933-79b13d340d2e,ca.m.9010,Mr. PETER HEENAN (Kenora-Rainy River):,,IS, 1926 16S7",,,"As a member representing, I think,

the largest constituency in that part of Ontario, I agree with a great deal of what has been said on the other side of the House, but. I have a suggestion that probably is the best one that has yet been made, and that is that we redistribute the whole of northern Ontario. Perhaps a committee appointed to do that work would be more appropriate. We in the Kenora-Rainy River district are not satisfied with the territory that has been alloted to us, and telegrams were sent to the Prime Minister at Ottawa shortly after the Redistribution bill went through. Some of the towns that had been included in the Kenora-Rainy River district for 'many years were cut off and put into the Port Arthur-Fort William territory, and now that they happen to have Conservative representation they are not at all happy.

775628,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.8.10,1926-03-18,4f144b8d-0f62-4502-b6eb-6bf2aa0faaad,ca.m.1477,Mr. MANION:,,IS, 1926 16S7",,,"That was Conservative

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Robert James Manion,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4f144b8d-0f62-4502-b6eb-6bf2aa0faaad&Language=E&Section=ALL
775629,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.8.11,1926-03-18,255d2664-d4b3-46aa-9933-79b13d340d2e,ca.m.9010,Mr. HEENAN:,,IS, 1926 16S7",,,"I was wondering if that

was the reason why my hon. friend (Mr. Manion) always answered when some hon. member called him the member for Rainy River. Now that those people have seen the light and have changed over from the representation they have had in the last ten years, I think northern Ontario should be redistributed in a proper manner. I agree with the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) that there is a great deal of misunderstanding and hardship in connection with the redistribution in northern Ontario, but just because an hon. member brings in a bill to strengthen one particular portion of it, and deal with that alone will not be satisfactory to northern Ontario as a whole. Consequently I would like my suggestion to be accepted, that we appoint a committee to redistribute the whole of northern Ontario.
Mr. J. R. O'NEILL (North Timiskaming): The riding which I represent is affected physically, but not on the basis of population. I descry in the suggestion of the hon. member

.for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) an appeal for the administration of extreme unction in his case. He refers to the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) taking unto himself the honour of representing Rainy River, but I think there is a great deal more in this suggestion than meets the ear, and so I would oppose the suggestion of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. I am in favour of the suggestion emanating from the hon. member for East Algoma, not that it affects my riding on the basis of population, but there is predominant in the minds of the people of that riding one idea, namely, that the redistribution of that territory constituted one of the crudest pieces of gerrymandering ever perpetrated in the political history of Canada. While that is a strong statement, and the hon. member for East Algoma was very generous in his suggestion in reference to the matter, I am rather inclined to think that if the situation were otherwise, hon. members on the opposite side of the House would be quite prepared to admit that something was radically wrong. The basis of revision may be in proportion to population at the present time, but the inaccessibility is such that it is practically impossible for the people represented there to reach their representatives without going out of their riding or out of the particular section of the country.
