775637,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.10.1.1,1926-03-18,090c4da7-b949-45d0-b63f-39854ba32056,ca.m.2263,Mr. A. W. NEILL (Comox-Alberni) moved:,,EXPLOITATION OF LABOUR,INDUSTRIAL FREEDOM OF CONTRACT AND ACTION,,That, in the opinion of this House, every effort should be made to affirm and establish the full industrial freedom of the citizens of Canada to bargain for their services on all industrial contracts and works; that the exploitation or conscription of labour should be prevented and condemned; that no person should be induced or compelled by undue influence, threats of dismissal, loss of wages or (position or (by any other unfair and improper (means, to .work for wages less than the standard or to engage in work which he has not agreed to do; that in all cases sueh wages as are generally accepted as current in each trade for competent workmen in the district where the work is carried out should be enforced and paid; and that this House will, so far as it is within the jurisdiction of parliament, endorse every reasonable and legtimate proposal to preserve such industrial freedom of contract and action, and will oo-operate with the several provinces in these objects to provide for uniform legislation throughout Canada.

He said; Mr. Speaker, this resolution is really very simple, and one which I am sure will readily receive support from all sides of the House, although perhaps its length and somewhat involved wording might give a different idea. The underlying principle is very simple. I had to have it somewhat loosely drawn, and expressed in somewhat [DOT].general terms, in order to bring it within the *scope of discussion in this House, otherwise -it. would have been framed in very much More simple language. Despite its general language, however, this resolution seems to have already given offence in some quarters.

I hold in my hand an editorial taken from a paper called The Gazette and presumably published in the city of Montreal, in which great offence is taken at this resolution. I have heard it said-I had no previous knowledge personally-that this paper is more or less devoted to what is known as the vested interests of Canada. If that is so, it certainly is anxious to prove its fidelity, because it is howling before anyone is hurt.

I see featured at the head of this editorial the fact that the paper was founded in 1778, 148 years ago, and apparently the political ideas current and acceptable then still hold sway in the editorial offices of this

paper to-day, 150 years later. The editorial is one long sneer, I might say, or one long attempt to be somewhat cheaply sarcastic at the expense of this resolution and of myself. I will leave out the personal allusions, which do not hurt me and will not interest this House. I notice repeated allusion in the editorial that they do not understand what the resolution means. If they do not understand what it means, why do they attack it? Why do they not wait until they get light on the subject; why devote a whole column of a so-called important paper in talking of ""hat they do not know? It almost suggests to the onlooker the old fashioned idea that to the ignorant everything unknown is suspicious, and therefore must be attacked.
I would just like to draw attention to one or two items; I would not think of delaying the House by reading all of it. The editorial says:
If be (Mr. Neill) is sincerely desirous o-f establishing industrial freedom, he will stop composing resolutions out of trades union catchwords.

And so on. I wonder what the really learned and capable King's Counsel who devoted a good deal of his time in drafting that resolution would say if he heard that his best success was a composition of trade union catchwords, whatever they may be. I do not think the editor would have used that language if he had known who really drafted that resolution. The ignorance displayed in the editorial is almost pitiable. It asks with fine sarcasm:
But when and how and where has labour in this country been conscripted?

I will show that presently, and to enlighten their ignorance I might say that it has been the law of the land for more than three years. Further they begin a discussion of the eight hour day; I do not know why, because it has nothing to do with my resolution. In putting up a man of straw in order to knock it down again, they say that no province of Canada has introduced the eight hour law. Poor, simple Gazette; they do not know that British Columbia has had that law on the statute books for several years. Again we find this gem, which is really worth consideration:
The individual workman has, and has always had, the abstract right to make the best of his market, to sell his labour upon fair terms or to withhold it.
Inferentially they imply ""What more does he want?"" I looked up in the dictionary the meaning off ""abstract"" and I find the word means ""existing in the mind only; not con-
Exploitation oj Labour
Crete'', so reading it with that meaning, the sentence would be:
The individual workman has, and has always had, the right existing in the mind only, not concrete, to make the best of his market, to sell his labour upon fair terms or to withhold it.

That might have been good political dogma 148 years ago, but the editor of this paper should remember that times have changed, and that we must move with the world or be left very much behind. What was extreme radicalism a few years ago is now being accepted by many of the Conservative governments of the world, and rights which exist only in the imagination are no longer satisfactory to the great body of the working people, who are more intelligent than they were 148 years ago. So much for The Gazette, with its ancient fossilized doctrines.

I think I can express in twenty words the real meaning of what I wish to bring before the House in this resolution. I will leave out everything else, and just recite those twenty words, taken from the resolution:
That the exploitation or conscription of labour should be prevented and condemned; that no person should be compelled to work for wages less than the standard

That, and that only, is the underlying motive o-f the resolution Which I am presenting to the House to-night. Before I deal particularly with the word ""conscription"", I wish to prevent any misunderstanding in regard to that word. I am not talking now of conscription in war time. So far as that kind of conscription is concerned, I am in favour of it, but I stand for conscription of all kinds; conscription of 4he millionaire as well as the pauper; conscription of capital as well as labour; conscription of the civilian at home as well as the man in the trenches, but I am not now talking about that kind of conscription of labour. I refer now to peace time conscription of labour. The Gazette wanted to know where and when and how labour was conscripted in peace time. If the editor of the Gazette will turn to chapter 93 of the Revised Statutes of British Columbia, 1924, he will find these words.

Any officer or employee of the Forest branch may employ or summon the assistance of any male person between the ages of eighteen and sixty, except only trainmen, telegraphers, and despatches on duty, doctors, and persons physically unfit-
They do not say anything about being mentally unfit.
.-for the purpose of controlling and extinguishing any fire, and the compensation for such voluntary or compulsory assistance shall be such as the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may provide.

They may take a judge from the bench or a member of parliament from his office and ' put him out to fight bush fires in the country. There is a rather serious penalty imposed of not less than $25 and not more than $100 in case of refusal to do so. That has been the law for the last three years.

Bush fires do not generally occur in towns, and consequently there is not much likelihood of professional and other people in urban centres 'being conscripted for fire-fighting purposes; the burden falls upon the country workers, and the remuneration that the government kindly accords them is 25 cents an hour, or $2 for an eight-hour day. That is not the current rate of wages in British Columbia.

I have before me an announcement that the scale of wages for the lowest outdoor labouring class in the city of Vancouver shall in the future be $4.50 a day; I think before that it was $4 a day. The government therefore makes a cut of 56 per cent in what is the current rate of wages in the city of Vancouver when they compulsorily conscript men to go out and fight fires. Then again it is not the $3.50 or $4 or $4.50 men generally upon whom this obligation falls. Naturally being in the buSh, it falls on men working in logging camps, such as trainmen, swampers and hook tenders, who get pretty high wages because they are engaged in dangerous and seasonal work which can be carried on only during a limited number of months each year. In the summertime they are laid off on account of danger from bush fires, and in the winter their operations are interrupted by heavy snow or rain; so when they are working, being highly skilled technical men, they get wages above the ordinary level, running from $5 to $9 a day. Suppose they are earning $6 a day, and are suddenly called off to work at $2 a day, that means a cut of 66 per cent. The Dominion government relieves itself of responsibility as regards its own employees by the fair wage resolution adopted by this House in July 1900, which was confirmed and made more effective by order in council in June 1922. We all know that this fair wage policy compels contractors and other employers to pay the current rate of wages for their particular trade in their particular locality.

Now, that is all I ask here, that when a man is taken against his will to fight bush fires he shall be paid the current rate of wages. Incidentally, I may say that this work almost invariably results in the destruction of his boots, and boots are costly in British Columbia. That, as I say, is all I suggest- these men should not be conscripted unless on the basis of their current rate of wages.
Exploitation of Labour
I am aware that this is not a matter in which this parliament can legislate, and that is why I have brought it up in this somewhat indefinite way. What I do want-

775638,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.10.1.2,1926-03-18,e59bd97e-ff2c-4d93-91cf-2c7d62ee9aac,ca.m.692,Mr. NICHOLSON:,,EXPLOITATION OF LABOUR,INDUSTRIAL FREEDOM OF CONTRACT AND ACTION,,Before the hon. gentleman leaves that point, may I ask, for information, whether he advocates by his resolution that authority to conscript men to fight bush fires in case of serious fire hazards in newly settled countries shall be taken away?

,Conservative (1867-1942),,George Brecken Nicholson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=e59bd97e-ff2c-4d93-91cf-2c7d62ee9aac&Language=E&Section=ALL
775639,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.10.1.3,1926-03-18,090c4da7-b949-45d0-b63f-39854ba32056,ca.m.2263,Mr. NEILL:,,EXPLOITATION OF LABOUR,INDUSTRIAL FREEDOM OF CONTRACT AND ACTION,,No, but I do not think men should be conscripted in times of peace at a compulsory wage fixed by the other party. They should be allowed an opportunity either to bargain for their wages, or in case of emergency they should be paid the standard wage that they are earning at their regular work. That is all I can ask this House to do. This being a matter of civil rights, I cannot ask that the provincial government shall be directed not to conscript labour for this purpose at less than the current rate of wages. I would only ask for expressions of opinion from the very able legal gentlemen on both sides of the House whether such legislation on the part of the local government is not really ultra vires. It would seem to me to be going beyond their jurisdiction. As far as civil rights are concerned, I am aware that it is within' their jurisdiction.

Apart from that, I would ask this House to at least go as far as to express moral disapproval of this action on the part of a provincial government, If it is legal and right in one-ninth of Canada to conscript men to fight fires at a wage to be fixed by those doing the conscripting, then by following the same logic it might be pronounced equally right to conscript men to cut logs or to do some other work which in the opinion of the authorities was needed at a wage which they considered should be such and so. In other words, I would point out that if the House passes this resolution it commits us to nothing except the expression of a sort of moral disapproval of conscripting men in times of peace to fight fires at a rate of wages from 50 to 66 per cent below the current wages in the locality for that kind of work.

,Independent,,Alan Webster Neill,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=090c4da7-b949-45d0-b63f-39854ba32056&Language=E&Section=ALL

ROBB (Minister of Finance) :,Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General,EXPLOITATION OF LABOUR,INDUSTRIAL FREEDOM OF CONTRACT AND ACTION,,There are some features of this resolution to which I take no exception whatever. But I notice in the first place my hon. friend says that the essence of his resolution is that the conscription of labour should be prevented and condemned, and if I followed him correctly, he finds some fault because in one of the provinces men are compelled to turn out and help fight bush fires. I cannot follow him that CMr. Neill.]
column2: I

column1: far. I think in times of such hazard the state must take some means to protect its property.
But there is another feature of his resolution which appeals to me:

That no .person should be induced or compelled by undue influence, ithreats of dismissal, loss of wages or position, or by any other unfair and improper means, to work for wages less than the standard or to engage in work which he has not agreed to do.

I find myself in sympathy with that part of the resolution to a certain degree because I have observed during a residence of some years in an industrial town and while going about the country in the recent general election that in certain industries notices sometimes are posted warning the employees that unless they voted in a particular way they will lose their position the day after the 9 p.m. election. It seems to me that every hon. member, no matter what party he supports, should repudiate such oppressive tactics on the part of large corporations. I do not mean to say that this applies particularly to federal elections. I have observed it even in municipal elections, when certain corporations were looking for concessions from the municipality.
So having that in mind, I am prepared to accept the resolution, for it covers an abuse that, it seems to me, should be corrected.

Mi-. E. B. RYCKMAN (East Toronto): Mr. Speaker, I have read this resolution for the first time, to-night. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has toldi us that a learned king's counsel drew it. I would like to know his name, because I think he was somewhat of a wag-that he tried to make fun of the hon. member. This resolution does not deal with matters within the competence of this parliament; it deals with matters within the competence of the provincial legislatures. Anything that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has saidi has related to a provincial statute, and the gravamen of the charge made by the hon. member is that in case of a conflagration endangering the safety of property, men should be allowed to stand idly by and not serve unless they have the dollars and cents passed over the counter to them. I am reminded of those ladies who were in a seminary which was burning up. It being after six o'clock at night when the firemen came up the ladders to rescue them, they declined to be rescued, unless the firemen were in evening dress. Such is the effect of this resolution. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that unless there is something that this august body has well within its competence it should not deal or attempt to deal with something that, notwithstanding

what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has said, is altogether outside the jurisdiction of this parliament.

775641,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.10.1.5,1926-03-18,e59bd97e-ff2c-4d93-91cf-2c7d62ee9aac,ca.m.692,Mr. G. B. NICHOLSON (East Algoma):,,EXPLOITATION OF LABOUR,INDUSTRIAL FREEDOM OF CONTRACT AND ACTION,,I have no objection whatsoever to the principle of this resolution, if there is a principle, but I do object to the affirmation of a principle condemning something that does not exist. As one who has had a life's experience in dealing with labour and workingmen's problems I say at once that in the province of Ontario at least and the parts of Canada in which I have had experience, no such condition exists. Men cannot be conscripted for ordinary labour against their will, nor can they be forced to accept wages that do not suit them.

With relation to the matter of fighting fires, let me just give you an illustration. We have had some harrowing experiences in recent years in the matter of fires in the part of Canada from which I come. Just recall, if you will, the fire at Haileybury, where about two o'clock in the afternoon a fire swept across the forest and wiped out that town completely. Would you say that the authorities of the town of Haileybury, or the provincial authorities represented there, should have to wait and start to bargain with people when they need their help to go and rescue the women and children whose homes were being devastated? That is what is involved in this resolution. So far as conscripting workingmen, and not the professional and business men, is concerned, again I say that no such condition exists. If you go back to the fires in Timmins, Englehart and Cochrane, when those towns were being wiped out it was the business men, the doctors, the lawyers, the clergymen, the railway officials and every other man who could go who went to the assistance of these people.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,George Brecken Nicholson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=e59bd97e-ff2c-4d93-91cf-2c7d62ee9aac&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Independent,,Alan Webster Neill,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=090c4da7-b949-45d0-b63f-39854ba32056&Language=E&Section=ALL
775643,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.10.1.7,1926-03-18,e59bd97e-ff2c-4d93-91cf-2c7d62ee9aac,ca.m.692,Mr. NICHOLSON:,,EXPLOITATION OF LABOUR,INDUSTRIAL FREEDOM OF CONTRACT AND ACTION,,Those who were unwilling were conscripted. The provincial government of Ontario places in the hands of those who are responsible for looking after fires in the north country authority to conscript men. The fire inspector has authority to come along to any man's plant, and take the superintendent of the sawmill, for instance, or the superintendent of a pulp mill and all his men, tie the whole plant up, and take the men to go and fight the fire. They do not, as my hon. friend says, pay them an arbitrary rate of wages of $2.50 a day. Not at all. The fire superintendent or the man in charge of the fire fighting forces of the provincial government has authority to pay these men what

they are worth and what they earn, and they pay extra money for this hazardous work. Why should we in this House of Commons pass a resolution that implies they are not doing that? That is the objection I have.

In so far as giving any man the freedom to bargain for any rate of wages he wishes to get, that is the recognized principle all over this country. There is no such thing as conscription of labour, nor is any effort made to hinder men from bargaining and getting everything they possibly can for their labour. That is recognized as their right; it has been so, and it will continue to be so. But do not let us place a stigma on the provincial authorities of a province just because certain conditions might obtain in some other province. If such conditions prevail elsewhere, then deal with the provincial authorities in that province.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,George Brecken Nicholson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=e59bd97e-ff2c-4d93-91cf-2c7d62ee9aac&Language=E&Section=ALL

MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,EXPLOITATION OF LABOUR,INDUSTRIAL FREEDOM OF CONTRACT AND ACTION,,The emphasis which is

being laid in this discussion on one particular phrase, not to say word, in the resolution which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has presented, is I fear directing attention away from the main purpose of the resolution. So far as there has been adverse criticism of what the hon. member has proposed, it has been to his including in his resolution the word "" conscription,"" and the conscription of labour referred to has been restricted to conscription in cases of fire. The hon. member has made his meaning quite clear. When he used the words ""exploitation or conscription,"" what he evidently intended to convey by the alternative word ""conscription"" was neither more nor less than what is conveyed by the word ""exploitation;"" and I would suggest to him, if that is what is in his mind, that it might remove any difference of view that the House may have on the essential parts of the resolution if he dropped the word ""conscription"" altogether, and just let that part of his resolution read ""the exploitation of labour should be prevented and condemned.""

I say this because I think the resolution itself is an important one and should be adopted by this House. It contains two or three fundamental principles on which all hon. members will, I trust, be prepared to agree. The first is a statement of the principle of freedom of contract and bargaining in the relations of capital and labour. That is a principle for which men have had to fight many industrial battles in the past, but which, happily, to-day is coming to be recognized as a principle which should be generally accepted. I venture to say there is not a member of this House who would stand up
Exploitation of Labour

in his place and say that he did not think it was in the interests of the community, as well as in the interests of capital and labour, that there should be the greatest freedom of bargaining in the making of contracts between the two great parties to industrial contracts.

,Liberal,,William Lyon Mackenzie King,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5&Language=E&Section=ALL
775645,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.10.1.9,1926-03-18,f33a161e-9b39-479e-aac0-a821d3eae7b1,ca.m.1704,Mr. RYCKMAN:,,EXPLOITATION OF LABOUR,INDUSTRIAL FREEDOM OF CONTRACT AND ACTION,,If the resolution is carried, will the Prime Minister bring in a bill embodying its terms?

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Edmond Baird Ryckman,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=f33a161e-9b39-479e-aac0-a821d3eae7b1&Language=E&Section=ALL
775646,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.10.1.10,1926-03-18,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Mr. MACKENZIE KING:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,EXPLOITATION OF LABOUR,INDUSTRIAL FREEDOM OF CONTRACT AND ACTION,,If my hon.

friend will be satisfied with half a loaf, instead of asking at once for a whole loaf, more progress will perhaps be made towards achieving what my hon. friend has in view. I take it that the view of the hon. member is this: In industrial questions, public opinion in the long run is more effective in achieving the object that is to be desired than mere legislation; that, after all, it is public opinion that will determine whether or not industrial laws will be respected. It is not the number of measures there may be on the statutes; it is rather the extent to which communities recognize that public sentiment is in accord with particular views.

My hon. friend has expressed two or three views here which it seems to me this parliament would do a national service in endorsing. One is the view already mentioned that there should be freedom of bargaining between capital and labour in the matter of industrial contracts. The second is that there should be no exploitation of labour, a term which I think is generally understood to mean the sweating of labour, employing labour under unfair conditions. The hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) has said that there is nothing of the kind in Ontario. I wish that could be said truly. I think there is less of it at present than there has been at any time heretofore, but I venture to say that all of the provinces of this Dominion present instances where labour is being sweated in a manner which I am sure all hon. members would do their utmost to stop if it were brought to their knowledge and attention. If this parliament expresses its view against the exploiting or the sweating of labour, public opinion formed on the basis of our expression of view may go far towards meeting the very object the hon. member has in mind in moving this resolution. The suppression of sweating is the second principle for which the resolution stands.
The third principle that my hon. friend affirms in his resolution is that of fair wages in contracts. He uses the phrase:
That the wages should be those that are generally accepted as current in each trade for a competent workman in the district where the work is carried out.

Now that phrase, as I recognize it, is one that has been in the public contracts of the federal government for the last twenty-five years. It was I think in 1900 that what is spoken of as ""the fair wages resolution"" was first introduced into this parliament. Since that time public contracts, whether they related to public works or to the making of uniforms for post office officials or for the militia, or any other form of public contract work-have contained clauses to prevent the sweating of labour and to secure for the labour engaged on these contracts the payment of wages at fair rates and the carrying out of the work under proper conditions. This House has already adopted a fair wages resolution, a resolution using the very language we are now asked to affirm. I might add that the resolution adopted originally by this House has in substance been adopted since by most if not all the legislatures of Canada with respect to the public contracts of the provinces. There is reason to believe that the resolution of this parliament has been copied by other countries as well. It is the power of example that my hon. friend is seeking to have exerted.

That brings me to the fourth point which my hon. friend mentions in his resolution, namely the importance of co-operation between the several provinces in order to secure uniform legislation throughout Canada. I might mention that, within the past four years, if I am not mistaken, we have already held a conference of the provinces under federal auspices to effect that very purpose. I believe that uniformity of industrial standards is one of the most important objects to be attained by legislation. In Canada it should be our aim to bring about, if at all possible, uniformity of legislation among the several provinces. It is important for this reason: if there is not uniformity it very often happens that the particular province that has higher standards in labour ultimately loses in consequence of the lower standards that exist in other provinces. The higher standard is undermined by the lower to the disadvantage of the particular industry which may be enjoying the highest standard. I remember some years ago looking into the question of sweating in industry, I found that in some of the American states where the clothing industry was carried on, that as one state raised its standards *of legislation with respect to fair working conditions the labour employed in that industry was gradually supplanted by labour enjoying a lower standard in another state, and the state that was really seeking to preserve a high -standard of labour was losing its industries.
Exploitation of Labour

as a consequence. Now the only way in which that sort of thing can be prevented is that there shall be like industrial standards over areas of effective competition however wide they may be. The League of Nations has seen the importance of that principle and has laid down in its labour clauses as an object to be aimed at the establishment of uniformity of industrial conditions not only as between the provinces of any one country but as between the different countries of the world; and I really believe it is a fact that until in some way the standards are made equal in the different countries, those countries that have higher standards are going to some extent to be handicapped in virtue of those very higher standards they have adopted.

I can perhaps illustrate what I mean by referring to what is known as ""Gresham's law of the precious metals"". It was discovered many years ago, in relation to matters of currency, that where there were the two metals in circulation, the baser metal tended to drive the better out of circulation, the coins made of metal of finer quality were hoarded or else were melted down and the metal used in the fine arts, and the coins made of the baser metal gradually replaced them in circulation. I believe that the so-called law of competing standards as applied to the precious metals is equally applicable in the matter of competing standards in industry, that where you have a lower industrial standard and a higher industrial standard competing with each other, the former tends to undermine the latter; the industry that is run on the lower standard will effectively and prejudicially embarrass that industry which seeks to support higher standards.

I believe speaking generally there is no country in the world that enjoys higher standards of industry than our own. From the national point of view, I believe there is everything to be said in favour of a resolution that will help to convey to the world the knowledge that the parliament of Canada supports the broad principle of uniformity of legislation with respect to fair wages with respect to conditions in industrial contracts, with respect to freedom from exploitation and with respect to freedom ^ in industrial bargaining. For that reason, for the moral support that parliament is able to give these great principles, I hope the House will adopt the resolution.

In so far as its specific terms go, were it a matter within our own competence I do not know that I would take any exception at all. It is all very true that the resolution says there shall be no conscription of labour, and that the member who moves the resolution in his interpretation of it himself declared that that should apply even to cases of extraordinary emergency such as a conscription to fight fire. The reading of the resolution itself does not necessarily embrace such a case at all, and I think the hon. member was poorly advised in going so far as to assert that he would strain his own words to the extent of saying that in the case of a great conflagration he would not have legislation on the statute book compelling the compulsory combating of that conflagration. Well, the conflagration is precisely of the same character; it is because it is of the same character that sometimes it becomes essential to resort to the same means. The reason is only too evident. It is because there can be no possibility of consideration or of bargaining on the one hand that it cannot be allowed on the other. The time does not permit of it; you cannot have it. Consequently the duty of the moment must be performed. All other rights must be submerged. As to the remuneration, that is a minor question. Something is to be said for a remuneration, something below the standard in a case of that kind. Nothing has been said in support of it, although I think something could have been. But it is not akin to the resolution, so I pass it by.

But the comment I want to make is this: Has the resolution any place in this parliament, and if so, does it become the government to pass its blessing upon it? I do not say that we have nothing at all to do with the question as to the fairness of wages. We have a little. We have to do with it only in so far as we employ the workers ourselves, in so far as we, the government, or we the parliament, in the case of our employees throughout the country can, directly or indirectly, influence contractors entering into engagements with us. To that extent we must take into consideration this principle regarding fairness to the wage earner. But the hon. member admits we have done that, and the whole House admits we have done it. Consequently there is no cause for castigation, there is no cause for any didactic resolutions or lectures; we are living up to the spirit of the law which the hon. member himself conceives to be right. So there is no reason for a resolution on that score. That is all we have to do with it. Over and beyond that, it is a matter for the provincial legislatures only. It is only within their jurisdiction. That is not a matter of dispute, for we all know it. Does it become this parliament to pass resolutions dictating to the provincial legislatures what kind of legislation they shall pass? Does the hon. member really think so? I do not think it does. The constitution of this country gives plenary powers to both sets of legislatures. The provinces are just as original in their jurisdiction as are we. Their powers are just as ample and just as plenary. We do not give them their powers; we cannot subtract from them. They are supreme in their own field just as we are supreme in ours. Have we no better task than to be entering upon their sphere of consideration, lending them a little of our wisdom and advising them what they ought to do? Is it dignified conduct? Does it become and befit the parliament of Canada? I suppose we could plead that they have offended in the same way-I know it was a very common practice of the legislatures of the prairie provinces to pass resolutions on the tariff, telling us what they wanted and what we ought to do here in the way of low tariff and no tariff. Hon. members were a whole lot freer in expressing themselves and putting themselves on record out there than they are when they get to the parliament of Canada. But they never achieved anything by it except perhaps a little local popularity. They were engaged in an exercise which could not be said to be worthy of a member of a local legislative assembly.

775670,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.11.1.1,1926-03-18,090c4da7-b949-45d0-b63f-39854ba32056,ca.m.2263,Mr. A. W. NEILL (Comox-Alberni) moved:,,MARKING OF EGGS,PROPOSED APPLICATION TO DOMINION OF BRITISH COLUMBIA ACT,,That, in the opinion of this House, it is desirable that the Eggs Marks Act of British Columbia should be made applicable to the Dominion of Canada as a whole.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am sure this resolution is in every respect the antithesis of the one we have just considered. It is short; it is simple; it is within our jurisdiction, and I think it will be acceptable to ever}rone. I might briefly explain how the need arises. There has been a continual feeling in British Columbia and no doubt in Ontario as well that the poultry farmers are not getting a square deal, owing to the importation] of American eggs. That leads one to the suggestion that there should be an increased duty on American eggs. As that is not the basis of this resolution, I am just alluding to it in passing.

Some months ago there was a meeting held at a place called Duncan in the riding of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie), which was attended by representatives of practically all the poultrymen of British Columbia. I may explain that the poultry industry in British Columbia is entirely different to that of any other province, inasmuch as it is a specialized business. There it is not a .case of having a few hens running around the farm machinery, nor is it a case where you can say to a man, ""Eggs are not selling well; you had better go in for cows."" You cannot do that when you have only five acres of land absolutely unsuited for anything else. Consequently they go in for specialized hen farms, with five or ten acres of land on which they keep from two to five thousand hens. It is useless to say to them that they should grow cucumbers or raise pigs, because the land is unsuited to that. At this meeting a number of resolutions were passed1; one asked for an increased duty on eggs coming from the United
Marking oj Eggs

States; another asked that there 'be no material change in, the egg grading regulations; a third resolution dealt with Australian eggs, and1 asked that they be not allowed to come in under the definition of ""fresh"", while the last, resolution was that which I just read. They asked that the Eggs Marks Act of British Columbia be made applicable to the Dominion as a, whole.

I may explain briefly what the act is. It was passed in 1923, and I need not quote it; in effect it states that every imported egg sold in British Columbia or offered for sale Shall have the country of origin stamped on each individual egg. That is, there must be a stamp stating that it comes from the country of origin. An egg from the United States would1 be marked ""U.S.""; an egg from China would be marked ""China"". That act was introduced three years ago, and I am advised that it has been exceedingly successful.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Donald Sutherland,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=39733e89-5c63-44ea-a981-bc71336702b7&Language=E&Section=ALL
775672,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.11.1.3,1926-03-18,090c4da7-b949-45d0-b63f-39854ba32056,ca.m.2263,Mr. NEILL:,,MARKING OF EGGS,PROPOSED APPLICATION TO DOMINION OF BRITISH COLUMBIA ACT,,The section is as follows:

Every egg dealer who keeps or has in his possession or under his control any eggs which have been imported into the Dominion, and which have not been marked, shall mark each egg with the words ""Produce of"", followed by the name of the country of origin of the egg.

It applies to every country outside of Canada. The result is, as I am advised by this association, that it has 'been of great assistance in preventing the importation of foreign eggs. Further, I am advised by the association as follows:

It is a well known fact in the business that the consumer is suspicious of a marked egg. About fifteen years ago this association placed its eggs on the market with a special stamp giving the name of the association and the producer's number, but it was found that occasionally a retail grocer would carry eggs in stock thus marked for some wreeks and some consumer would purchase a dozen of these stale eggs and forever forswear anything with the Cowichan Creamery stamp on it. We know of one firm of distributors in Vancouver that made an attempt to bring marked eggs before the public, and for the same reason gave up in disgust.

The idea, of course, is that a man might import perfectly fresh eggs from the United States ; he might put them at the back of the bin and put eggs received later in front, and in that way the eggs first received might become more or less stale. Then when a consumer buys an egg marked "" U.S. "" or whatever it might be and does not like it. he tells his wife not to buy any more of that kind. Then there is another idea, that when an egg is marked as being from a foreign country, the suggestion is that it might possibly not

be fresh, coming from that distance. People do not stop to consider whether ""US."" means the state of Washington or the state of California. Also, it is possible that some vague spirit of patriotism stirs the man at his breakfast and he says to his wife, "" Get local eggs if you can; I see these are imported.""

775685,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.11.1.16,1926-03-18,090c4da7-b949-45d0-b63f-39854ba32056,ca.m.2263,Mr. NEILL:,,MARKING OF EGGS,PROPOSED APPLICATION TO DOMINION OF BRITISH COLUMBIA ACT,,I will deal with that again later. Discussing for the moment the cost of marking these eggs, this association says that to mark eggs arriving in this country in accordance with the act would not cost more than one cent a dozen. So the cost to the
Marking oj Eggs
consumer would be negligible. The association adds:
Since the act went into force in British Columbia, eggs imported from Washington are seldom sold in British Columbia, being generally bought for re-shipment elsewhere.
They do not appear to have found any trouble in British Columbia. There is a penalty provided in the act for anyone who exposes eggs for sale that are not so marked:
Anyone who violates any of the provisions of this act is liable to a fine not exceeding $100.

This is something practical; it, has been in existence in British Columbia for three years and has been a pronounced success. There are no complaints from the consumer. The legislation has not raised the cost of eggs to him, but it has raised their quality, and he likes it. He buys more eggs now, the consumption in British Columbia having gone up considerably. It does not hurt the dealer, for he passes on the cost-and it is trifling. But it helps the producer because it tends to keep out foreign eggs. My hon. friends opposite, who are such enthusiastic exponents of protection, will kindly take notice that this is a form of protection without increasing the cost to the consumer of the commodity protected. and yet it is claimed that such legislation will materially benefit the producer for it gives his eggs a preference over the American. If any further explanation is desired I shall be happy to furnish it when I close the debate. This is fundamental: The policy has been a success in British Columbia; it is not going to cost anybody anything; and it will help the struggling poultry interest not only in that province but here as well.

MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):,Minister of Agriculture,MARKING OF EGGS,PROPOSED APPLICATION TO DOMINION OF BRITISH COLUMBIA ACT,,Mr. Speaker, so far as the Eggs Marks Act of British Columbia may come under federal jurisdiction, I think there is no objection to the resolution. For the last eight or ten years every egg-exporting country has been making commendable efforts to improve the quality of its product. In Canada the first effort I recall was during the war-I think part of the time under the old Canada Food Board-with good results; but that applied only I think to export eggs. This resolution is restricted to imported eggs, and the main purpose is that of identifying the country of

origin, so that the source of all imported eggs will be known, this information appearing on the egg itself, on the container, and on a placard to be displayed where the eggs are retailed. Having regard, however, to the fact that some of the regulations we introduced three years ago are not yet sufficiently known to warrant any change-it is generally accepted that any regulation should be in force for two or three years at least to give it a fair trial- it is not the intention of the government to make any changes in those regulations until another year has elapsed.

With that understanding, and with the further understanding that we would not incorporate any provincial law inconsistent with federal jurisdiction, there can be no objection to this resolution going through.

column1: Section 5, subsection 1, providles:

Every person (being the proprietor of any manufactory, bakery, confectionery, hotel, restaurant, cafe, tea room, or any place or shop where any Chinese eggs are exposed or offered for sale, or used in the preparation of any goods, wares or merchandise, or used in the preparation of any food exposed or offered for sale or served for meals, shall place a legible sign in some conspicuous place where all persons entering his place of business can readily see the same, upon which is marked in letters not less ,than four niches high the words, ""Chinese eggs used here"" or, ""Chinese eggs sold here"", as the case may be.
Now, there is no reference there to the importation of egg's from the United States or from Hong Kong. A great many more
Marking oj Eggs
eggs arrive here from Hong Kong than from China, and I do not know that there is any great difference between the eggs coming from those two sources.

,Independent,,Alan Webster Neill,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=090c4da7-b949-45d0-b63f-39854ba32056&Language=E&Section=ALL

I do not think he caught my remarks. If he looks at section 3 of the act which he has in his hand he will find that the importation of eggs from any place outside Canada is fully covered. ,Independent,,Alan Webster Neill,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=090c4da7-b949-45d0-b63f-39854ba32056&Language=E&Section=ALL
775693,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.11.1.24,1926-03-18,39733e89-5c63-44ea-a981-bc71336702b7,ca.m.2365,Mr. SUTHERLAND (South Oxford):,,MARKING OF EGGS,PROPOSED APPLICATION TO DOMINION OF BRITISH COLUMBIA ACT,,I

was directing attention to something that my hon. friend neglected to point out to the House when he was dealing with the resolution, that is, the particular pains taken to make it appear that eggs from China are being used in the restaurants of this country, and that no such pains are taken with respect to eggs from Hong Kong. Now, a great many more eggs arrive from Hong Kong than from China. I fail to see why a distinction should be made between eggs from those two sources. I might refer to subsection of section 5 of the British Columbia act. Apparently in British Columbia there is a very strong feeling against anything imported from China. If my hon. friend is so anxious to nrevent unfair competition from other countries, I think he should be equally eager to see that the poultry raisers of British Columbia are protected from that great country to the south just as much as from Hong Kong, China, and any other country.

I have here figures of the importation of eggs from the United States, and they show that during the three weeks of February some 820,000 dozen eggs were imported into Canada from the United States. The British Columbia Act provides against the importation of eggs only from China; why single out China? Section 5 of the British Columbia Act mentions nothing except the importation of eggs from China. It is true, as my hon. friend has pointed out, that under section 3 of that act the eggs have to be marked. In restaurants where eggs are used in the making of pastries and other things of that kind a card has to be exhibited showing that the eggs used are from China, if that is where they are from. Why not exercise equal vigilance with regard to eggs from the United States or any other country? If our eggs in Canada are so superior-and in the view of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) they must be, because he has passed regulation after regulation until the people engaged in the raising of poultry in this country are completely paralysed; I venture to say there is not one man in fifty, no, not one
[Mr. D. Sutherland.!

in a hundred or nine hundred of those engaged in poultry raising who understands the regulations of the Department of Agriculture to-day-if, I say, our eggs are so superior, why not take the same precautions against the eggs from other countries that you take against the eggs imported from China?

And now to make the situation still more complicated the hon. member asks to have the act of British Columbia made applicable to the eggs which are imported into this country. If he would exercise the same precautions with regard to eggs from all countries as he does with regard to eggs from China, I would be heartily in accord with him. I think it is absolutely necessary that we should know where the eggs come from. The Minister of Agriculture this afternoon, when the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) called his attention to the importations of dairy products into this country, could not answer at the moment, but wanted time to consider and find out whether the products of other countries were being sold in this country as Canadian products. I think the minister must be aware of the facts in view of the representations which have been made to his department. I think he must also be aware that grave complaints have been made with regard to the importation of eggs. I do not see why China should be singled out and the eggs from other countries, the United States, Australia and the rest of the world, be allowed to escape.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Donald Sutherland,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=39733e89-5c63-44ea-a981-bc71336702b7&Language=E&Section=ALL

Section 3 is not applicable in this respect at all. Section 5 is the one that makes it necessary to put up cards in the restaurants if the eggs used there come from China.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Donald Sutherland,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=39733e89-5c63-44ea-a981-bc71336702b7&Language=E&Section=ALL
775696,ca.proc.d.1926-03-18.11.1.27,1926-03-18,d8e64909-c88d-4e3e-abfe-a46943452386,ca.m.3572,Hon. J. W. EDWARDS (Frontenac-Adding-ton):,,MARKING OF EGGS,PROPOSED APPLICATION TO DOMINION OF BRITISH COLUMBIA ACT,,Mr. Speaker, I have only a word to

say. Marking of Eggs

stead of benefited. I agree with the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) that there are already too many regulations in force with regard to the grading of eggs. Under the existing regulations eggs when they enter Canada, whether from China or other countries, are examined as they come through the customs. Not only are they graded, but the quality is marked on the cases, not on the eggs. I believe that is a sufficient safeguard if the idea is to protect our poultry industry.

As the hon. member for South Oxford says, if the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) would adopt some procedure whereby the householders would know what kind of eggs they were buying, it would be a step in the right direction. As matters are at present the householder may think he is buying a first grade egg when as a matter of fact it is an egg of the third grade and is not to be compared in quality with the egg it is supposed to represent. The present trouble is caused by too many regulations and too many grades. As to the requiring the dealer to stamp the eggs, I really believe he has so much to do at present that such a thing is out of the question. In the case of eggs coming from China or the United States they at least should be stamped by the producer in the country from which they come. If that were done the consumer would know when he was eating a Chinese egg, but the stamping should be done by the man in China.

The producers in Canada are not worrying about the competition caused by eggs from China. Those eggs cannot come through the customs as first grade eggs because they are too old to meet the requirements of that grade; therefore Chinese eggs must be classed as thirds. If people want to buy such eggs they should do so after the grade of third had been stamped on them and also the country of origin. That would remove a lot of the difficulty complained of. If the hon. member for ComoxnAlberni would exclude these inferior eggs from Canada altogether, or impose a sufficiently high duty, it would be a benefit to the Canadian poultry industry. The reason those engaged in that industry cannot make both ends meet is because of the unfair competition to which they are exposed, and the present multiplicity of grades. The grades should be properly arranged and simplified so that people will know what kind they are buying. A Canadian egg of the first quality will offer convincing proof of its merits.
Mr. HARRY J. BARBER (Fraser Valley): Let me say in the first place that I am in sympathy with the resolution. During a

I do not think we need worry about the marking of the individual egg. I know one firm in the city of Seattle who claim that they have no objection to the marking of individual eggs for export into Canada, and the cost would not be over one-half cent per dozen. Therefore I think there is no need for concern over the question of the stamping of the individual egg. We have found in British Columbia that we have little or no trouble. There eggs when put on sale must be marked with the country of origin, so that when the customer comes to buy eggs he or she knows that they are from the United States, or from China, or whatever the country of exportation may be. That system has worked out well in my own province.

I returned from British Columbia this morning, and let me assure my hon. friend (Mr. Neill) that he is not going to solve all the problems of the poultryman through the instrumentality of his resolution. During my recent visit to British Columbia I travelled through some of the outlying districts, and they were bringing eggs in and selling them at the low rate of fifteen and twenty cents a dozen, and at the same time paying a big price for feed. In addition to the marking of eggs I think it is absolutely necessary that there should be an increase of duty. I believe the hon. .member said some time ago that he was quite favourable to bringing the Canadian tariff on eggs to a parity with that of the United States provided that it did not 'interfere with the policy of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). Deputations waited on me urging that course while I was there, and I have had communications

I think my hon. friend has also received some-in which the raising of the tariff is urged. In addition, the adoption of the eggmarking act of British Columbia was advocated. We have got to accord some protection to the poultryman. I am going to support the resolution, but I hope . before the session closes the government will grant some further protection to the poultry industry by making our tariff equal to that of the United States.

column2: That a petition has been, within the time specified in 'the Corrupt Practices Inquiries Act, being chapter 8 of the Revised Statutes of Canada (1906) as amended, presented to the House of Commons signed by mors than twenty-five electors of the electoral district of Athabaska, stating that no petition charging the existence of corrupt practices has been presented under the Dominion Controverted Elections Act, and that corrupt or illegal practices have, or that there is reason to believe that corrupt or illegal practices have extensively prevailed at the election holden 'in the said electoral district of Athabaska aforesaid on the 29th day of October, 1925.

column1: He said: Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to take up any time in discussing this motion. I rise merely for the purpose of moving it. The motion has been on the order paper for six weeks, and covers practically all the arguments that I would care to make on the question this evening. The Corrupt Practices Inquiries Act, chapter 8 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, as amended, provides for an inquiry into alleged corrupt and illegal practices under certain conditions. More than twenty-five electors of the federal electoral district of Athabasca have petitioned this House praying for an inquiry under the terms of the statute. The petition was accepted by this House on the 1st February and I move this motion at this stage simply in order to give effect to the prayer of that petition.

Before the House adjourns every evening leaders on both sides, after the motion is put, speak on matters quite different from the motion to adljourn, and by the courtesy of the members, and by custom from time immemorial, no one has ever taken any objection to that. There is no question before the Chair at the present moment. The Minister of Finance evidently did not notice that the adjournment of the House had been moved and that I was about to declare the
Supply-Point of Order

motion carried. He then inquired about his motion, and I declared that the motion could not be moved. So this is a tempest in a teapot, if I may say so, with all due deference, and without any vindictive spirit. It is well known that every evening before the House adjourns, when the motion is put and often after it has been declared carried, the leaders in the House put questions to each other as to the business for the next day.
